questions.prompt: According to Lesson 1, why is scaling an AI system NOT simply "the same system, but bigger"?
options: New failure modes, cost dynamics, and organizational dependencies appear at scale that were structurally impossible to encounter at prototype scale
Scaled systems always use a completely different programming language than their prototypes
Scaling only ever changes the user interface, never the underlying architecture
A working prototype guarantees the same code will work identically in production
questions.explain: Lesson 1 names four dimensions that genuinely change at scale: load, failure modes, cost, and organizational surface area -- none of which show up meaningfully at prototype volume, which is why prototype success proves the approach works but not that it will hold up in production.

questions.prompt: Northbeam's assistant handles 2,000,000 requests/day. An engineer adds 400 tokens to the system prompt, which would normally pass code review without a second glance. Why does this deserve real scrutiny at this scale?
options: The small per-request cost increase gets multiplied by 2 million requests every day, turning an invisible-looking change into roughly $876,000 of extra annual cost
Adding tokens to a system prompt is always a sign of a security vulnerability
400 tokens always costs exactly the same dollar amount regardless of request volume
This change has no real cost impact because system prompts aren't billed by token count
questions.explain: Lesson 2's worked example shows exactly this: a per-request cost that's negligible in isolation becomes a large, real financial number once multiplied by production volume -- the core reason cost budgets have to be set and watched explicitly at scale.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about capacity planning, per Lesson 3.
options: The lead time a fix requires -- not just the date a capacity ceiling will be hit -- determines when the work actually needs to start
Capacity planning should always maximize headroom regardless of cost, with no tradeoff to consider
Projecting growth forward is more actionable than only measuring current load
The correct amount of infrastructure headroom depends on the real business cost of an outage, which differs between an internal tool and a customer-facing product
questions.explain: Lesson 3 is explicit that capacity planning is a tradeoff between over-provisioning cost and under-provisioning risk, not a rule to always maximize headroom -- the right amount depends on what an outage actually costs the business, and lead time (not just the ceiling date) drives when work must start.

questions.prompt: Two regions each run independently at 99.9% uptime. Lesson 4 shows their combined uptime can reach 99.9999% -- but only under what condition?
options: The two regions' failures must be genuinely independent -- a shared dependency (same model API account, same auth service) silently breaks this assumption
Both regions must be operated by the exact same engineering team
Both regions must use identical hardware from the same vendor
The condition only applies if both regions are in the same country
questions.explain: The redundancy math assumes independent failure probabilities; a shared upstream dependency reintroduces a single point of failure that silently invalidates the combined-availability calculation, which is why real HA design spends real effort removing shared dependencies.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 5's case study shows that the SAME architecture choice (like multi-region deployment) can be exactly right at one growth stage and ________ at an earlier one, which is the real skill being tested in a 'how would you scale this' interview question.
questions.explain: The lesson's central point: architectural complexity should match actual current scale -- building Stage 4's full HA architecture at Stage 1 (100 users) would have been wasted effort solving a problem that didn't exist yet.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks how you'd scale a RAG system from 100 to 1,000,000 users. Per Lesson 5, what distinguishes the strongest answer from a weaker one?
options: Narrating the stages and the specific trigger for each architectural change, rather than describing one maximally robust architecture as if it should have existed from day one
Describing only the final, most sophisticated architecture possible, regardless of what each growth stage actually needed
Listing as many distributed-systems buzzwords as possible
Refusing to discuss cost or latency, since those are implementation details
questions.explain: Jumping straight to the most advanced-sounding architecture reads as inexperience; explaining what changes and why at each stage demonstrates the actual judgment this course is teaching.

questions.prompt: According to Lesson 6, why is the 'Alternatives Considered' section of an ADR often more valuable than the 'Decision' section itself?
options: The most common question a Staff/Principal engineer gets asked is 'why didn't we choose the other option,' and this section answers it without requiring anyone to reconstruct the reasoning from memory later
Alternatives Considered is required by law for all technical documents
The Decision section is always factually less accurate than the Alternatives section
ADRs without an Alternatives section cannot be saved in version control
questions.explain: Lesson 6 frames this as the section most ADRs skip and the one that matters most -- it prevents wasted time re-evaluating an already-rejected option and gives a ready answer to the question people ask most often.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 7's worked example, building a re-ranker in-house came out $26,400 cheaper over 2 years than buying it as a managed API. What does the lesson say about treating this cost comparison as the final answer?
options: Non-cost factors (speed to market, team expertise and risk, vendor dependency risk, whether the capability is a differentiator or commodity) can still make buying the right call despite the higher cost
The cheaper option by raw cost is always correct, with no other factor worth considering
This result proves that buying is never worthwhile for any AI component
The calculation must contain an error, since managed services are always cheaper than building in-house
questions.explain: Lesson 7 is explicit that cost alone isn't the whole decision -- speed to market, team expertise/risk, vendor dependency risk, and differentiator-vs-commodity status all belong in the decision alongside the raw numbers.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the weighted scoring matrix technique from Lesson 8.
options: The weights assigned to each criterion are usually where the real judgment call lives, not the scores themselves
Two engineers can score every option identically and still recommend different options, purely because they weighted criteria differently
A close result between top options is meaningless and should be ignored
A sensitivity check reveals whether a recommendation is fragile (flips with small weight changes) or robust
questions.explain: Lesson 8 explicitly treats a close scoring result as valuable information -- it signals the decision is genuinely sensitive to the weights -- and recommends a sensitivity check specifically to learn whether the ranking is fragile or robust.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, what is the single most common reason a design document stalls in review?
options: Presenting only one option with no alternatives forces reviewers into an all-or-nothing choice, so partial objections have nowhere to go except a full rejection
The document is formatted in Markdown instead of a word processor
The document is reviewed by too many people at once
The document doesn't include a cover page or table of contents
questions.explain: Without visible alternatives, a reviewer with a real but partial objection can't say 'I prefer this over the alternatives, but address X' -- they're stuck between full approval and full rejection, which stalls the decision.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 9 recommends including a '________' section in a design doc, stating explicitly what the design deliberately does NOT attempt to solve, to prevent reviewers from debating a problem the document never claimed to address.
questions.explain: The Non-Goals section scopes the proposal explicitly, heading off one of the most common ways design reviews get derailed.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 10's case study, Weaviate scored highest (7.50) for Northbeam's specific weights, narrowly beating Pinecone (7.40). What would make a DIFFERENT company's situation legitimately favor Pinecone instead, without Weaviate's win being "correct" universally?
options: A smaller team with less appetite for operating any infrastructure might weight operational simplicity more heavily, favoring Pinecone's fully managed model
Pinecone can only ever score higher if Weaviate is discontinued as a product
The scoring matrix always produces the same winner regardless of any company's actual priorities
No other company situation could ever produce a different ranking than Northbeam's
questions.explain: Lesson 10 is explicit that the scores reflect Northbeam's own judgment call for their specific situation -- a team with even less operational appetite would weight operational simplicity more heavily, which could flip the ranking toward Pinecone.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 11, what real cost does a senior engineer create by answering every technical question fastest in every meeting, even when every individual answer is correct?
options: The team quietly learns that waiting for the senior engineer is more efficient than reasoning it through themselves, and the team's own judgment never develops
The senior engineer's own technical skills decline as a direct result
There is no real cost -- faster correct answers are always strictly better for a team
This habit always causes the senior engineer to be promoted faster
questions.explain: Lesson 11's named failure mode: reflexive deference develops quietly, and a team whose senior engineer leaves can suddenly struggle with decisions it used to make easily, revealing those decisions were never really the team's own.

questions.prompt: An architecture review ends with "great discussion, lots to think about, let's reconvene." Per Lesson 12, why has this review failed even though the conversation was substantive?
options: The review's actual purpose was to reach one of three concrete outcomes (approved, approved with changes, rejected) and the meeting ended without landing on any of them
The review succeeded, since a substantive discussion is itself the goal of any review
The review failed only because fewer than five people attended
Reviews should never involve any back-and-forth discussion at all
questions.explain: Lesson 12 frames an architecture review's purpose as reaching a decision, not having an interesting conversation -- ending without a concrete outcome means the review didn't do its actual job.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about mentoring through a hard technical problem, per Lesson 13.
options: Immediately solving a mentee's bug for them is usually the fastest fix but can leave them less prepared for the next similar bug
A narrowing question (e.g., 'does this reproduce under concurrent load?') models the kind of reasoning a skilled debugger uses, without stating the answer directly
A mentor should always withhold the direct answer regardless of how stuck or time-pressured the mentee is
Letting a mentee take a genuinely low-cost wrong turn can sometimes teach more than redirecting them immediately
questions.explain: Lesson 13 explicitly rejects a one-size-fits-all rule -- when a mentee is genuinely blocked, time-pressured, and has exhausted their own ideas, withholding the answer stops being mentorship and starts being an unnecessary cost.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, why does re-litigating a lost architecture argument in a smaller side conversation damage a team's decision-making beyond just failing to change the outcome?
options: It introduces the risk that any future decision could be reopened through a side channel instead of staying settled, which makes the team move slower on ALL decisions, not just the contested one
Side conversations are always more technically rigorous than the original decision meeting
This behavior has no real effect on the team beyond the one decision being re-argued
Re-litigating a decision always reverses the original outcome
questions.explain: Lesson 14's core point: once a team learns decisions can be reopened through side channels, trust in ALL settled decisions erodes -- the damage generalizes well beyond the one re-argued issue.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, when should 'disagree and commit' be replaced with escalation instead?
options: When the disagreement involves serious, hard-to-reverse consequences -- a security vulnerability, a compliance violation, or a choice extremely costly to undo once committed
Disagree-and-commit should never be replaced with escalation under any circumstances
Escalation should be used for every single technical disagreement, regardless of stakes
Only when the disagreeing engineer has more years of experience than the decision-maker
questions.explain: Lesson 14's test: if being wrong would cause an absorbable, learnable cost, disagree-and-commit fits; if being wrong would be genuinely difficult to undo, escalation to someone with authority to revisit the decision is the right move instead.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 15's likelihood/impact/________ framework for communicating risk to non-technical stakeholders ends with a specific request for what decision the listener should actually make.
questions.explain: Likelihood (how often), impact (what happens), and ask (what decision is being requested) are the three components -- without the ask, a listener is informed but has nothing concrete to act on.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, what does 'blameless' actually mean in a blameless postmortem?
options: The investigation focuses on the systemic reasons a mistake was possible and reached production, rather than assigning individual fault -- it doesn't pretend no human error occurred
No one is ever allowed to acknowledge that a mistake happened at all
Only the most senior engineer present is permitted to speak during the postmortem
Blameless postmortems skip root-cause analysis entirely
questions.explain: A postmortem culture that punishes the individual teaches people to hide mistakes and near-misses -- blameless redirects the investigation toward fixable systemic causes instead, which is what Lesson 16's 5 Whys example demonstrates.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 16's 5 Whys example, the surface explanation for Northbeam's incident was "a bad deploy." What was the REAL root cause five steps down?
options: There is no process that periodically re-samples test data to keep it representative of the growing production knowledge base
An engineer was simply careless and should be formally reprimanded
The vector database vendor's service was fundamentally broken
The company does not employ enough engineers
questions.explain: Each 'why' pushed past the surface explanation to a specific, fixable process gap -- the missing test-data resampling process -- rather than stopping at a vague, unenforceable conclusion like 'review code more carefully.'

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, why does the lesson recommend enforcing a standard with tooling (a CI check) wherever possible, instead of relying on a human reviewer's memory?
options: A tooling-enforced standard gets followed consistently because it doesn't depend on anyone remembering anything, while human-enforced standards are followed inconsistently
Tooling-enforced standards are always technically impossible to implement in practice
Human reviewers always catch every violation without exception
Tooling enforcement eliminates the need to ever write the standard down
questions.explain: Lesson 17's point: a CI check that blocks a pull request closes the gap that human vigilance alone leaves open, since reviewers are busy, tired, or new and will miss things no matter how well-intentioned they are.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 18's technical-debt break-even calculation only answers whether a refactor is worth it once you also know how long the affected code will actually remain in active use -- the lesson calls this distinguishing code cleanliness from code ________.
questions.explain: Even very messy code isn't worth refactoring if it will be retired before the fix's cost is recovered -- longevity, not cleanliness alone, determines whether the break-even math actually pays off.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 19, why does the prompt-assembly refactor belong on Northbeam's roadmap BEFORE the hybrid-search initiative, even though leadership never asked for the refactor?
options: The refactor is a real, identified dependency for hybrid search -- building hybrid search on the current duplicated logic would mean implementing it five times instead of once
All technical debt must always be addressed before any new feature work, with no exceptions
The refactor was secretly part of the original business goal all along
Dependency-driven sequencing is only relevant for infrastructure projects, never feature work
questions.explain: Lesson 19's sequencing point: a roadmap that only lists metric-moving items without surfacing real technical dependencies risks discovering blockers mid-quarter instead of planning around them up front.

questions.prompt: Per the capstone (Lesson 20), what is the actual point of writing your own ADR for the confidence-threshold scenario, as distinct from matching the model answer's exact conclusion?
options: Reasoning the way the model answer reasons -- naming real trade-offs honestly and being explicit about what's unknown -- which can legitimately lead to a different, equally defensible conclusion under different assumptions
Memorizing the model ADR's exact wording for future recall
Always agreeing with whatever conclusion the model answer reaches, regardless of the scenario's specifics
Avoiding any mention of cost, latency, or team expertise in the written decision
questions.explain: The capstone is explicit that a different, well-justified conclusion (e.g., assuming more labeled data already exists) is a legitimate success -- the exercise tests the reasoning process, not an exact match to one conclusion.
